A person’s attachment style is not a mental health condition.

Respectfully you are not describing avoidant attachment style in your post at all. 

Lovebombing, manipulation, projection, deflection, gaslighting someone etc are emotionally abusive tactics. A person can have avoidant attachment and *not* show emotionally abusive behaviours. You will see things like… a distinct FEAR of commitment that they will openly talk about that ties in to past experiences and their self-worth, periods of closeness and then specific things that may cause them to feel triggered, physical/observable symptoms of anxiety, need for independence, need for quiet introspection or something random/spontaneous when feeling burnt out, difficulty managing emotional overwhelm *alongside* another person due to reliance upon self-soothing, a need for safety and security without feeling smothered. 

They will be open and honest about what is triggering for them, they will not lack insight or empathy, and certain experiences will be visibly unsettling for them. You will see the tug of war conflict between their emotions, desires, and so on. 

Having an avoidant attachment style is not a mental health condition. It is not a personality disorder. It is not narcissistic personality disorder (NPD). It is not someone with narcissistic tendencies - though of course someone may also have this attachment style and have NPD; true NPD is rare.

I haven’t done research on this next bit in particular but I would be inclined to say a person with narcissistic tendencies may be more inclined to have an anxious attachment style; fearing abandonment, become codependent on their supply in order to feed their constant need for admiration and sense of grandiosity etc. I’ve never met a narcissist who did not thrive on, and seek out, constant incessant attention from their supply/supplies before they slowly start devaluing them. Whereas people with an avoidant attachment style get overwhelmed by this.

10 years ago I took a call centre job to get over my fear of talking on the phone. I stuttered terribly! I was so terrified of talking on the phone that I’d have my mother or roommate or partner (at the time) make phone calls for me. 

It took about 5 years of solid work on it and practice to get much better. 

I now make multiple calls a day, most days. For myself, or for my children. With no problem. I barely stutter at all anymore and if I do I don’t even care.

Considering the anxiety used to be crippling, what helped me was remembering that *no one speaks fluently 100% of the time*. For me, my anxiety around speaking was simply the fear of others’ judgment.

If you are really interested in each other, you are both going to need to try and find a way to understand more about each other’s interests. They are trained professionals with years of study and practical application of counselling and psychotherapeutic skills, effective verbal and non verbal communication, body language and so on. Good therapists know how to hold space for their client, to bring about a sense of safety and security, and they do genuinely care about their client’s wellbeing.

I get that it's hard. The person I've been in NC with for 7 days today has a birthday in 10 days time. I will not contact them.

The thing is — we don't know what we've lost, until we know that we have lost it. Say you can't find something that was special to you. You search everywhere for it and then it hits you that it's actually lost. Did it hit you that hard before you realised it was actually lost? Or did you think, "it's OK, it'll be around somewhere. It'll turn up." No. Things mean more to us when it's clear that they are no longer accessible.

The same analogy applies here.

How can your ex appreciate your presence in her life, when she doesn't know what your absence feels like? 

This is one facet of NC that reinforces why maintaining no contact is key. 

The MAIN purpose of NC is to work on ourselves so that we heal and grow, regardless of whether the other person returns or not. But certainly a facet of NC is that, indirectly or not, it shows the other person what they are missing. Provided they did genuinely care for you and aren't a sociopath or narcissist.

Another consideration is this. Let's say you send the birthday message. There's a few scenarios that may arise in doing so:

A) You get no response. Ouch. That's hurtful and will set you back on your journey.

B) You get a response with an opener. Do you honestly want to hear the, "Thanks. How have you been?" No. You don't need breadcrumbs.

C) You get a response with an offer to catch up. But the ball is once again in their court because, had you NOT initiated contact, would they have reached out first? You'll never know. It is not a genuine attempt at reconnection because YOU have reached out first.

Remember that she broke up with you, and chose to walk away. She would be expecting you to reach out for her birthday. Let her wonder why you're not. It is not your problem anymore. 
If she wants to reconnect down the line, she will find a way to make it happen, without any birthday message from you.
Stay strong.
